{{about|limits of sequences of generalized functions|limits of probability distributions|Convergence of random variables#Convergence in distribution}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in the theory of [[generalized function]]s, the '''limit of a sequence of distributions''' is the distribution that sequence approaches. The distance, suitably quantified, to the limiting distribution can be made arbitrarily small by selecting a distribution sufficiently far along the sequence. This notion generalizes a [[limit of a sequence|limit of a sequence of functions]]; a limit as a distribution may exist when a limit of functions does not.

The notion is a part of distributional calculus, a generalized form of [[calculus]] that is based on the notion of distributions, as opposed to classical calculus, which is based on the narrower concept of [[function (mathematics)|function]]s.

== Definition ==
Given a sequence of distributions <math>f_i</math>, its limit <math>f</math> is the distribution given by 
:<math>f[\varphi] = \lim_{i \to \infty} f_i[\varphi]</math>
for each test function <math>\varphi</math>, provided that distribution exists. The existence of the limit <math>f</math> means that (1) for each <math>\varphi</math>, the [[limit of a sequence|limit of the sequence]] of numbers <math>f_i[\varphi]</math> exists and that (2) the linear functional <math>f</math> defined by the above formula is continuous with respect to the topology on the space of test functions.

More generally, as with functions, one can also consider a limit of a family of distributions.

== Examples ==
A distributional limit may still exist when the [[classical limit]] does not. Consider, for example, the function:
:<math>f_t(x) = {t \over 1 + t^2 x^2}</math>
Since, by [[integration by parts]],
:<math>\langle f_t, \phi \rangle = -\int_{-\infty}^0 \arctan(tx) \phi'(x) \, dx - \int_0^\infty \arctan(tx) \phi'(x) \, dx,</math>
we have: <math>\displaystyle \lim_{t \to \infty} \langle f_t, \phi \rangle = \langle \pi \delta_0, \phi \rangle</math>. That is, the limit of <math>f_t</math> as <math>t \to \infty</math> is <math>\pi \delta_0</math>.

Let <math>f(x+i0)</math> denote the distributional limit of <math>f(x+iy)</math> as <math>y \to 0^+</math>, if it exists. The distribution <math>f(x-i0)</math> is defined similarly.

One has
:<math>(x - i 0)^{-1} - (x + i 0)^{-1} = 2 \pi i \delta_0.</math>

Let <math>\Gamma_N = [-N-1/2, N+1/2]^2</math> be the rectangle with positive orientation, with an integer ''N''. By the [[residue formula]],
:<math>I_N \overset{\mathrm{def}} = \int_{\Gamma_N} \widehat{\phi}(z) \pi \cot(\pi z) \, dz = {2 \pi i} \sum_{-N}^N  \widehat{\phi}(n).</math>
On the other hand,
:<math>\begin{align} \int_{-R}^R  \widehat{\phi}(\xi) \pi \operatorname{cot}(\pi \xi) \, d &= \int_{-R}^R \int_0^\infty \phi(x)e^{-2 \pi I x \xi} \, dx \, d\xi + \int_{-R}^R \int_{-\infty}^0 \phi(x)e^{-2 \pi I x \xi} \, dx \, d\xi \\
&= \langle \phi, \cot(\cdot - i0) - \cot(\cdot - i0) \rangle
\end{align}</math>
